CHEB, CHEBIL: a quill pen cut for writing.

CHECAY: fresh fish, recently caught or not spoiled.

CHECECH, CHECECHIL: scar, the mark of a wound or sore.

CHECECH: See *chikich.*

CHECOLKAX: forest cut down for a <term>milpa</term> <gloss>maize field</gloss> or sown plot.

CHECH: one who cries a great deal, for no reason.

CHECH, CHECHIL: smaller than others; *u chechil chich, u chanchanil;* the smallest of the birds. Obsolete.

CHECHÉ: raw, neither cooked nor ripened. See *che muy,* its synonym.

CHECHECUNTAH: v. a. to harden.

CHECHEH: bare and ringing, like coins, maize kernels, bones.

CHECHEHAH: v. a. to make coins clink by jingling them. | To heft maize so that it sounds dry and solid, or similar things.

CHECHEHBIL: a thing that has been or must be made to clink or ring, like metals, grains, bones, etc.

CHECHEHCUNZAH: v. a. to give something the quality of clinking or ringing, like coins, grains, bones, etc.

CHECHEHCI: a thing that rings like very dry and solid maize, coins, etc.; also things crowded and packed together, like trees laden with fruit.

CHECHEIL: what is raw, and rawness.

CHECHEHEL: what is crowded or packed very close.

CHECHEK: trampled, p. p. of *cheechek.*

CHECHEKAH: v. a. to trample.

CHECHEKAHAN: p. p. of *chechekah.*

CHECHEK-OCTAH: to trample.

CHECHEPOC, CHECHEPOCAH: to sear meat lightly <note>original: "perdigar," to brown meat briefly before cooking it fully</note>.

CHECHETAL: to stay raw, not to cook through.

CHECHETAC: things that are not cooked.

CHECHELTAL: See *chichiltac.*

CHECHIL: a child's very persistent crying.

CHECTETAH: v. a. to search for.

### CHEE

CHEE: interjection, "God help me!" | Laughter. See *ché.*

CHEEBAK: raw meat. See *chechebak.*

CHEECAY: See *checay.*

CHEECH: a crybaby who cries over nothing.

CHEECHBAC: sardine.

CHEECHCUNTAH: to make someone into a crybaby.

<column-break/>

CHEECHEK: trampled.

CHEECHEKAH: v. a. to trample, to tread underfoot.

CHEECHIL: the habit of crying over little or nothing.

CHEECHTAL: v. n. to acquire the habit of crying over little.

CHEEH, CHEEHNAHI: v. n. to laugh.

CHEEH, CHEEHIL: laughter.

CHEEHBIL: laughable, worthy of laughter.

CHEEHBOZ: See *chehboz.*

CHEEHEL: v. n. to pile up like chains or bare bones; for bones to show through from thinness.

CHEEHTAH: v. a. to laugh at something.

CHEEHTAHAAN: p. p. of *cheehtah.*

CHEEHTABIL: See *cheehbil.*

CHEEHTZIL: laughable, worthy of laughter.

CHEEKTAL: v. p. to laugh at another, to mock; to be greeted with laughter.

CHEEKEL: v. n. to be trodden; for a female animal to be covered by the male. | To fertilize the female.

CHEEKIK: fresh or raw blood; although it is given as a synonym of *cheecay.*

CHEEL: staff, walking stick, the same as *ché.*

CHEEL: rainbow. See *chel.*

CHEEL: the highest part, or the part with least water, in the <term>cenotes</term> <gloss>natural sinkhole wells of Yucatán</gloss>. See *cheh.*

CHEEN: a very familiar word for pleading with someone or for reproaching them, added like an interjection. *Cóten cheen! Luken cheen!* "Come on! Get away!"

CHEETAL: v. n. for a pulpy or starchy root to turn woody.

### CHEH

CHEHAN: p. p. of *chehtal:* piled up like bones, money, etc.

CHEHAH: for chains to clank as they pile up; to make coins clink.

CHEHBA: v. reciprocal. To crowd together; for the bones to show through from thinness.

CHEHBIL: coins that have been or must be jingled on top.

CHEHBOZ: a rock in the sea.

CHEHCUNZAH: v. a. to pile up bones, money, etc. | For the bones to show through a great deal.

CHEHCUHTAHAAN: p. p. of the preceding.

CHEHECBAL: for chains to be piled up. | For bones to show through.

CHÉHEL: p. p. of *cheehel;* piled up.

CHEHENCHEH: chains piled up; bones exposed from thinness.

6. Bücheler reads ὄφρα for ἤ ῥα, making Apollo the subject of ἐχάλασσε and ἐκλήϊσε. The common reading is preferable.
8. **τόξον**: the “bow” must include the quiver, which alone, to speak properly, is hung on the back of Apollo. **πρὸς κίονα πατρὸς ἑοῖο** is briefly put for “the pillar against which stood his father’s seat.” So Arete sits κίονι κεκλιμένη, ζ 307, and Odysseus sits πρὸς κίονα μακρήν, ψ 90. In both cases the pillar is near the hearth, and appears to be the place for the master or mistress of the house. In θ 65 f. the herald puts a seat for Demodocus against a pillar, on which he hangs the lyre of the minstrel.
10. **νέκταρ**: cf. the scene of the gods drinking nectar in Δ 1 f.
11. Gemoll objects to the usual punctuation (adopted in the text), on the ground that the order should be ἔνθα δ᾽ ἔπειτα, and that in Ο 86 all the gods pledge Hera. He therefore punctuates at the end of the line, supplying a verb for δαίμονες from δεικνύμενος. But the point is that the gods remain standing until Apollo is seated; and this is best brought out by the punctuation of the text. **ἔνθα** is emphatic in this position: “then and not till then,” *tum demum*.
13 = 126.
14–18. This invocation has been suspected by many commentators, who think that it is the beginning of a hymn to Leto (or a complete hymn). According to Ilgen it may have been interpolated

owing to the similarity of χαίρει δέ τε πότνια Λητώ to χαῖρε κτλ. But there is no good reason why Leto should not be honoured in a hymn addressed to her son, and the invocation is not unsuitable at this place.
14. **μάκαιρ᾽ ὦ Λητοῖ**: for the formulaic order cf. *Eur. Bacch.* 565 μάκαρ ὦ Πιερία, *Ar. Nub.* 1205 μάκαρ ὦ Στρεψιάδες, *Orph. h.* iii. 12 μάκαιρ᾽ ὦ Νύξ. The position of ὦ is Homeric; e.g. Δ 159, δ 26, θ 408, σ 122, υ 199, xxvi. 11. The order is not found in Attic prose. (In *Plat. Euthyd.* 271 c Stallbaum reads θαυμασία, ὦ Κρίτων for θαυμάσι᾽ ὦ Κρίτων.) For later poetry cf. *Anth. Pal.* vi. 239. 1 ἀγρονόμ᾽ ὦ Πάν.
15. It is natural to mention both the children of Leto, although the hymn is addressed to one of them. Artemis is joined with Apollo in the invocation at 165, where see note.
16 = *Orph. h.* xxxv. 5. **Ὀρτυγίῃ**: hardly the Syracusan Ortygia, as Fick (*Odyssee* p. 281) supposes, although that place was closely associated with Artemis; see *Pind. Nem.* i. 1 f., *Pyth.* ii. 7. Delos itself was anciently called Ortygia (schol. Apoll. Arg. A 419, Athen. ix. 392 D and in Alexandrian poetry e.g. *Callim. h. Ap.* 59, followed by *Verg. Aen.* iii. 124, Hesych. s.v. Ὀρτυγία, Eust. 1558), but the islands are here expressly distinguished; cf. *Anth. Pal.* vi. 273 Ἄρτεμι Δᾶλον ἔχουσα καὶ Ὀρτυγίαν ἐρόεσσαν. We may here follow Strabo (x. 5. 5), who identifies Ortygia with Rheneia. The Ortygia of o 404 is unknown. For further references see Preller-Robert i.

# III TO APOLLO

She <note>Leto</note> unstrung his bow and closed his quiver,
and taking it from his strong shoulders with her hands,
she hung the bow against a pillar of his father
from a golden peg; and she led him and seated him on a throne.
<margin>10</margin> Then his father gave him nectar in a golden cup,
welcoming <note>original: "δεικνύμενος"</note> his dear son, and then the other gods
sit down there; and queenly Leto rejoices,
because she bore a bow-bearing and mighty son.
Hail, O blessed Leto, since you bore glorious children,
<margin>15</margin> Lord Apollo and Artemis the shooter of arrows,
the one in Ortygia, and the other in rocky Delos,

6. **truly then** <note>original: "ἤ ῥα"</note>] **until** <note>original: "ὄφρα"</note> Bücheler    7. **with her hands** [corrupt form] L    8. **hung up** [incomplete] L : **the bows indeed** Stoll : **and the bows** Schneidewin || **before** <note>original: "πρὸ"</note> EL    9. **seated** [variant spelling] M    11. **and** <note>original: "δὲ"</note> omitted in pH    12. **queenly** [incomplete] L    14. **blessed Leto** [variant case] M

6. Bücheler reads "until" <note>original: "ὄφρα"</note> for "truly then" <note>original: "ἤ ῥα"</note>, making Apollo the subject of the verbs "unstrung" and "closed." The common reading is preferable.
8. **the bow** <note>original: "τόξον"</note>: the “bow” must include the quiver, which alone, to speak properly, is hung on the back of Apollo. **against a pillar of his father** <note>original: "πρὸς κίονα πατρὸς ἑοῖο"</note> is briefly put for “the pillar against which stood his father’s seat.” So Arete sits "leaning against a pillar" <note>original: "κίονι κεκλιμένη"</note>, *Odyssey* 6.307, and Odysseus sits "against a tall pillar" <note>original: "πρὸς κίονα μακρήν"</note>, *Odyssey* 23.90. In both cases the pillar is near the hearth, and appears to be the place for the master or mistress of the house. In *Odyssey* 8.65 f. the herald puts a seat for Demodocus against a pillar, on which he hangs the lyre of the minstrel.
10. **nectar**: cf. the scene of the gods drinking nectar in *Iliad* 4.1 f.
11. Gemoll objects to the usual punctuation (adopted in the text), on the ground that the order should be "then and thereafter" <note>original: "ἔνθα δ᾽ ἔπειτα"</note>, and that in *Iliad* 15.86 all the gods pledge Hera. He therefore punctuates at the end of the line, supplying a verb for the **gods** <note>original: "δαίμονες"</note> from the word for **welcoming** <note>original: "δεικνύμενος"</note>. But the point is that the gods remain standing until Apollo is seated; and this is best brought out by the punctuation of the text. **then** <note>original: "ἔνθα"</note> is emphatic in this position: “then and not till then,” <note>Latin: "tum demum"</note>.
13 = 126 <note>Note: This indicates line 13 is identical to line 126 of the hymn.</note>.
14–18. This invocation has been suspected by many commentators, who think that it is the beginning of a hymn to Leto (or a complete hymn). According to Ilgen it may have been interpolated

<column-break/>

owing to the similarity of "and queenly Leto rejoices" <note>original: "χαίρει δέ τε πότνια Λητώ"</note> to "hail [blessed Leto]" <note>original: "χαῖρε κτλ."</note>. But there is no good reason why Leto should not be honoured in a hymn addressed to her son, and the invocation is not unsuitable at this place.
14. **O blessed Leto** <note>original: "μάκαιρ᾽ ὦ Λητοῖ"</note>: for the formulaic order compare Euripides, *Bacchae* 565 "O blessed Pieria" <note>original: "μάκαρ ὦ Πιερία"</note>, Aristophanes, *Clouds* 1205 "O blessed Strepsiades" <note>original: "μάκαρ ὦ Στρεψιάδες"</note>, *Orphic Hymn* iii. 12 "O blessed Night" <note>original: "μάκαιρ᾽ ὦ Νύξ"</note>. The position of "O" <note>original: "ὦ"</note> is Homeric; e.g. *Iliad* 4.159, *Odyssey* 4.26, 8.408, 18.122, 20.199, and Hymn 26.11. The order is not found in Attic prose. (In Plato, *Euthydemus* 271 c Stallbaum reads "wonderful one, O Crito" <note>original: "θαυμασία, ὦ Κρίτων"</note> for "O wonderful Crito" <note>original: "θαυμάσι᾽ ὦ Κρίτων"</note>.) For later poetry compare *Greek Anthology* vi. 239. 1 "O Pan of the fields" <note>original: "ἀγρονόμ᾽ ὦ Πάν"</note>.
15. It is natural to mention both the children of Leto, although the hymn is addressed to one of them. Artemis is joined with Apollo in the invocation at line 165, where see note.
16 = *Orphic Hymn* xxxv. 5. **Ortygia**: hardly the Syracusan Ortygia, as Fick (*Odyssey* p. 281) supposes, although that place was closely associated with Artemis; see Pindar, *Nemean Odes* 1.1 f., *Pythian Odes* 2.7. Delos itself was anciently called Ortygia (Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius, *Argonautica* 1.419, Athenaeus ix. 392 D and in Alexandrian poetry e.g. Callimachus, *Hymn to Apollo* 59, followed by Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.124, Hesychius under the entry "Ortygia", Eustathius 1558), but the islands are here expressly distinguished; cf. *Greek Anthology* vi. 273 "Artemis who holds Delos and lovely Ortygia." We may here follow Strabo (x. 5. 5), who identifies Ortygia with Rheneia. The Ortygia of *Odyssey* 15.404 is unknown. For further references see Preller-Robert volume i.

### XXX. To make Manmene <gloss>g</gloss>.

Take the thighs <gloss>h</gloss> or the flesh of capons, boil <gloss>i</gloss> them, and carve them small into a mortar. Take milk of almonds with broth of fresh beef and put the flesh into the milk or the broth. Place it on the fire and mix it together with flour of rice or of wheat, thickened like the 'blanc de sure', and with the yolks of eggs to make it yellow, and saffron. When it is dressed in dishes with 'blanc de sure', sprinkle upon it cloves <gloss>k</gloss> and sprinkle upon it powder of galantine, and serve it forth.

### XXXI. To make Bruet of Almayne <note>German broth</note>.

Take roasted partridges, chickens, and roasted quails, and larks boiled. Dismember them and make a good caudle <note>a warm, spiced drink or sauce</note>. Dress the flesh in a dish and sprinkle powder of galantine thereupon. Stick in cloves and serve it forth.

Take chickens or hens or other flesh and make the color as red as any blood. Take pepper, cinnamon, and gingerbread <gloss>l</gloss> and grind them in a mortar

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of a previous set of questions to a new series based on Aristotle’s "De Caelo" (On the Heavens). It marks the beginning of the First and Second Questions regarding optical properties and the natural motion of the four elements.</meta>

From the book "On the Heavens" <note>original: "Kitab al-Sama'," referring to Aristotle's treatise "De Caelo," which discusses the nature of the universe and the four elements.</note> regarding Aristotle, he began the response to the other questions with the permission of God the Almighty.

**The First Question**

If there is a clear, white, spherical glass vessel filled with clear water, it takes the place of a spherical crystal in causing combustion <term>al-ihraq</term> <note>the focused point of heat produced by a lens or burning-sphere.</note>. If the vessel is empty of clear water and contains only air, it does not cause burning and does not collect the light rays. Why does water perform this action while air does not? And why does this burning and the collection of rays occur?

**The Answer**

Water is a dense, heavy body that possesses a slight color in its essence. The denser a body is, the more light reflects from it. Therefore, the light reflects from the glass <margin>which is densely packed</margin> when it is filled with water. A strong burning occurs as a result of this powerful reflection <note>Though the author uses the term "reflection" (in’ikas), the phenomenon described is refraction. Medieval scientists often viewed the bending of light through a dense medium as a form of redirection or reflection toward a central point.</note>. As for air, it is not a substance from which light reflects, nor does light reflect within it, because air is truly transparent. Therefore, if there is air in the glass, no strong reflection occurs from it.

**The Second Question**

Which of these two views is correct? One speaker says that water and earth move toward the center, while air and fire move away from the center. Another says <margin>among them</margin> that all the elements move toward the center, but the heaviest of them simply precedes the lightest in its movement toward it.

**The Answer**

The statement of the second opponent is false. If fire moved toward the center, it would either reach the center during its motion or it would never reach it. If it never reaches it, then it is not truly moving toward it.

<summary>This page addresses why water-filled glass spheres can focus light to start fires while air-filled ones cannot, and debates whether all elements naturally move toward the center of the universe.</summary>

**As for the first**, there are three things in it: its first water, which is the child;
its earth, which is the mother; and the mixture of the two, in the regimen of sevens.
**The second** is the same, in the regimen of tens. **The third**
is the same, in the regimen of fours. Each one has three
principles: a child, a mother, or a mixture of both. Jābir
said: I say, regarding the work we are engaged in, namely setting
the difference: whoever takes the water that dissolved in seven
days and dissolves with it the earth from the regimen of ten
days, and takes the earth that coagulated in seven and dissolves it
with what dissolved in ten days, two mighty, great elixirs result,
each of which dyes greatly.
The one whose earth is from ten and whose water is from seven: one part dyes
fifteen thousand. The one whose water is from ten
and whose earth is from seven: one part dyes twelve thousand.
If they are mixed in combination, the water of what was managed in four days with the earth
of what was managed in seven, and the earth of what was managed in four with the water of what was managed
in seven or ten, they dye as follows: what has earth of four
and earth of seven, one part dyes seven thousand; what has earth
of ten, one part nine thousand; what has earth of seven
and water of four, one part eleven thousand; and what has earth
of ten, one part thirteen thousand. In this there is precious knowledge,

<summary>Jābir lists the three components of each regimen (water as child, earth as mother, and their mixture) and gives the dyeing strength of elixirs made by crossing the waters and earths of the seven-, ten- and four-day regimens, ranging from seven thousand to fifteen thousand.</summary>
